ch1.title: Actuality and potentiality, side by side
ch1.caption: The one distinction the whole proof runs on. Actuality is how a thing already is; potentiality is the range of ways it could be but isn't yet.

columns.label: Actuality
columns.sub: the way a thing already is, right now
items: The coffee is actually hot — steaming at 90 °C
The ball is actually round and actually red
You are actually awake, actually reading this line
Only what is actual can do anything to anything

columns.label: Potentiality
columns.sub: the ways it could be, but isn't yet
items: The coffee could go cold — it really can do that
The ball could be squashed flat, or could bounce
You could learn Greek; you haven't yet
A potential, just as potential, does nothing at all

ch1.note: A potential is not nothing: the coffee can grow cold but cannot turn into chicken soup, and that difference is real. But a potential is not yet something either — so it cannot make itself actual. That single point is the hinge of the whole argument.

ch1.title: Drill: actuality or potentiality?
ch1.caption: Eleven everyday items. Decide whether each names how something already is, or a way it merely could be.
ch1.prompt: Is this an actuality or a potentiality?

items.text: The rubber ball's roundness
items.why: It is round right now. That is simply how the ball actually is.

items.text: The rubber ball's squashability
items.why: Nothing is squashed yet. It names a way the ball could be if something squashed it.

items.text: The heat of the coffee that is steaming in front of you
items.why: The heat is there, doing work — warming the cup, rising as steam.

items.text: The coldness the same coffee will have in an hour
items.why: Not nothing — this coffee really can cool — but not real yet either.

items.text: The acorn lying in your palm
items.why: It is actually an acorn. Whatever else it might become, it is this now.

items.text: The oak tree that acorn could grow into
items.why: A genuine potential of the acorn, and not of a pebble — but no oak exists yet.

items.text: Your ability to speak a language you have never studied
items.why: You could learn it. Until you do, the ability is only potential.

items.text: Your understanding of this sentence as you read it
items.why: It is happening. An actual act of understanding, not a mere capacity.

items.text: The flame on a match that is already lit
items.why: Actually burning, and able to set other things alight.

items.text: An unstruck match's capacity to start a fire
items.why: Real, but merely potential — which is why the match cannot light itself.

items.text: The statue still hidden inside the uncarved block of marble
items.why: The marble can be carved into it. Until a sculptor acts, there is no statue.

ch1.title: What change turns out to be
ch1.caption: Parmenides argued that change is impossible because it would mean something coming from nothing. Aristotle's reply rescues change — and hands us the tool the proof needs.
ch1.where: Stage 1: Change is real, and cannot coherently be denied

nodes.text: The coffee is hot; its coldness does not exist
So (says Parmenides) the coldness is nothing at all
And nothing cannot become something
nodes.note: So Parmenides concludes that the coffee cannot really grow cold, and that change of any kind is an illusion.

nodes.text: But no one can coherently believe that
nodes.note: Following his argument from premise to conclusion — being unconvinced, then convinced — is itself a change. Denying change takes changing your mind.

nodes.text: And the coldness was never simply nothing
nodes.note: This coffee can grow cold; it cannot fuel a car or turn into chicken soup. Something in it marks off the first from the others.

nodes.text: It was there potentially, though not yet actually
So change is a potential in a thing being made actual
nodes.note: Nothing comes from nothing — because a potential is not nothing.

ch1.title: Why change needs a changer
ch1.caption: The principle of causality is not a guess from many observed cases. It falls straight out of what change was just shown to be.
ch1.where: Change requires a changer: the principle of causality

nodes.text: Change is a potential being made actual
A potential, just as potential, does nothing
nodes.note: The coffee's merely potential coldness cannot cool anything — that is exactly what being merely potential means.

nodes.text: Only what is already actual can do anything
So nothing can actualize its own potential
nodes.note: It would have to be actual already in the very respect in which it is only potential.

nodes.text: Whatever goes from potential to actual is actualized by something already actual
nodes.note: This is the principle of causality. The cool air already actually cool, the ice cube already actually cold.

nodes.text: Note the claim is NOT 'everything has a cause'
nodes.note: It is narrower: whatever is actualized has an actualizer. Remember this when someone asks what caused God.

ch1.title: A linear (per accidens) series
ch1.caption: The familiar kind of causal chain, stretching backwards in time. Each member has its own causal power, so the earlier ones can vanish and the rest carries on.
ch1.where: Linear series stretching back in time

links.note: The cool air around it is drawing the heat away.

links.text: …because the air in the room is cool
links.note: And the air keeps its coolness for a good while all by itself.
It goes on cooling whether or not anyone is still in the house.

links.text: …because you pressed the button an hour ago
links.note: You could have walked out or dropped dead a second later; the cooling would carry on regardless.

links.text: …because the sun had made the room uncomfortable
…and so on backwards, perhaps with no beginning at all
links.note: Aristotle himself thought the world had always been here. The proof does not need a first moment, and does not claim one.

ch1.collapse: Pull the earliest member out and nothing greys out: each link already has its power built in and keeps working without its predecessor. That is why a series like this needs no first member.

ch1.title: A hierarchical (per se) series
ch1.caption: The cup, the desk, the floor, the foundation, the earth — all at once. Here every link but the last is only passing along a power it does not have on its own.
ch1.where: The hierarchical series: cup, desk, floor, earth

links.text: The cup sits three feet above the floor
links.note: Its potential to be up there is being actualized — right now, not at some past date.

links.text: …only because the desk is holding it up
links.note: A desk has no power of its own to hold anything aloft; it would fall too.

links.text: …only because the floor is holding the desk up
…only because the foundation is holding the floor up
…only because the earth is holding the foundation up
links.note: Within this everyday series the earth acts as the 'first' member: it holds without being held. Feser notes even the earth is not first in the strict sense — that comes later.

ch1.collapse: Take the earth away and every link above it goes slack in the same instant. The desk and floor were never lifting anything on their own; they were instruments, like a brush in a painter's hand.

ch1.title: Drill: which kind of series is this?
ch1.caption: The test is not 'is it simultaneous?' but 'does each member have its causal power on loan?' Twelve real examples to sort.
ch1.where: Taking stock: the hierarchical series is more fundamental

items.text: A train of carriages, each pulled by the one ahead, engine at the front
items.why: No carriage pulls under its own steam. Uncouple the engine and the whole train stops at once.

items.text: A father, his father, and his father before him
items.why: A man can father children long after his own father is dead. The power to beget is his own, not borrowed.

items.text: A hand moving a stick that pushes a stone
items.why: The stick pushes only while the hand pushes it. Its power is borrowed moment by moment.

items.text: A chandelier hanging from a chain fixed to the ceiling
items.why: The chain holds nothing by itself. Cut the ceiling fixture and chain and chandelier fall together.

items.text: Your mind being kept in existence at this very instant
items.why: Whatever holds you in being has to be doing it now. A cause that finished its work centuries ago would not keep you here.

items.text: A shove that topples the first of a hundred dominoes
items.why: Sweep the shover away and the dominoes keep falling. Each has its own weight and momentum.

items.text: Your grandmother taught your mother a recipe, who taught you
items.why: You can cook it tonight with both of them gone. The knowledge is now yours.

items.text: A motor turning a gear, which turns a gear, which turns a gear
items.why: Every gear turns only while the motor drives the train of them. Cut the power and all stop together.

items.text: The air conditioner that cooled the air that cooled your coffee
items.why: Once the air is cool it goes on cooling the coffee even after the unit is unplugged.

items.text: A painter, a brush, and paint going onto canvas
items.why: It is not the brush that paints, but the painter using it. The brush is an instrument here and now.

items.text: An oak grown from an acorn dropped by an older oak
items.why: The parent tree can be firewood by now. This oak grows by its own nature.

items.text: The subatomic particles making your atoms be atoms right now
items.why: Not a story about the past: it is what makes your body be a body at this instant, and it depends on deeper levels in turn.

ch1.title: From change to existence: what holds the coffee in being?
ch1.caption: The same hierarchical pattern, but now about existing rather than about location. Not 'how did the coffee get made?' but 'what keeps it being coffee at this instant?'
ch1.where: From change to existence: what keeps the coffee in being right now?

links.text: The coffee exists, here and now
links.note: Brewing it this morning explains how it got here, not what keeps it in being at this moment.

links.text: …only because the water in it exists now
…only because these atoms are bonded as water now
links.note: The very same matter has the potential to be loose hydrogen and oxygen instead. Why is the water potential the one being actualized?

links.text: …only because subatomic parts compose those atoms now
links.note: Naming a deeper particle only moves the question down a level; it never answers it.

links.text: Something that actualizes without being actualized
links.note: It cannot merely happen to lack a cause. Having no potential for existence at all, there is nothing in it that could need actualizing. Pure actuality.

ch1.collapse: Remove the bottom member and there is no coffee, no water, no atoms — not eventually, but at that very instant. Everything above was borrowing its existence.

ch1.title: Why a hierarchical series cannot run on forever
ch1.caption: Not because infinity is impossible — Feser allows infinite series elsewhere — but because borrowers cannot lend what none of them owns.
ch1.where: Why a hierarchical regress can’t be infinite — and two misfiring objections

nodes.text: In a per se series every member but the first has borrowed power
Borrowed power has to be borrowed from something
Adding more borrowers never produces a lender
nodes.note: A paintbrush cannot move itself, and it would be no more able to if the handle were infinitely long. Length is beside the point.

nodes.text: Mirrors reflecting mirrors forever still need a face
nodes.note: Otherwise there are images of nothing. The face supplies content it did not get from another mirror.

nodes.text: So the series needs a member whose power is built in
nodes.note: 'First' here means non-derived, not earliest. It is first the way the painter is first, not the way 1 is first in 1, 2, 3.

nodes.text: Misfire 1: 'but infinite mathematical series exist'
nodes.note: True and irrelevant — no instrumental causes there, indeed no causes at all. Aristotelians never banned infinite series as such.

nodes.text: Misfire 2: 'but the universe may be beginningless'
nodes.note: Also allowed. That is a claim about a linear series in time, and this argument never needed a beginning.

ch1.title: Stage 1, end to end
ch1.caption: The whole first half of the proof in nine steps, from a cooling cup of coffee to a purely actual actualizer.

nodes.text: Change is real — denying it is itself a change of mind
Change is a potential being made actual
No potential actualizes itself; only what is actual actualizes
Anything that changes must exist in order to change
nodes.note: Nonexistent coffee cannot cool, or do anything else.

nodes.text: Its existing at this moment is itself a potential being actualized
So right now something is actualizing its existence
That actualizer is either being actualized in turn, or purely actual
This series is hierarchical, so it cannot regress forever
So there is a purely actual actualizer — no potentiality at all
nodes.note: An unactualized actualizer: Aristotle's Unmoved Mover, stated precisely.

ch1.title: Stage 2: everything that follows from pure actuality
ch1.caption: Each attribute is derived the same way — assume God lacked it, and you find yourself attributing an unrealized potential to something that has none.
ch1.where: Stage 2: Why call it God? Immutability, eternity, immateriality

root.note: Nothing in it is merely potential. There is no unrealized potential anywhere in it to be found — that single fact does all the work below.

branches.why: To change is to have a potential actualized. It has no potentials, so there is nothing in it that could change.
Existing in time entails being changeable. It cannot change, so it does not exist within time: no beginning, no end, no before and after.
To be material is to be changeable and in time. It is neither, so it is not made of matter.
A body is a material thing, and this is not material, so it has no body of any kind.
Two of a kind need something to tell them apart, and any difference means one has what the other lacks — an unrealized potential. There can be no second.
An imperfection is a privation: some potential a thing should have realized and hasn't. There are no unrealized potentials here.
A thing is good insofar as it realizes the potentials of its nature, bad insofar as it fails to. Nothing is left unrealized, so nothing is deficient.
To have power is to be able to actualize potentials. Every actualizing power anywhere traces back to this one source, so it has all power there is.
It causes every kind of thing there could be, and a cause must contain what is in its effects. So every pattern is in it — held abstractly, the way ideas are held in a mind.
If the patterns of everything that exists or could exist are in its thought, then nothing whatever falls outside the range of that thought.

ch1.title: Objection anatomy: 'What caused God?'
ch1.caption: The most popular objection to any first-cause argument, and the one that misses hardest. Watch where the premise gets swapped.
ch1.where: ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’
ch1.says: If everything has a cause, then God has a cause too. And if you're allowed to say God just doesn't have one, why can't I say the universe doesn't have one? You're making an arbitrary exception to save your conclusion.
assumes: That the argument's premise is 'everything has a cause'
That God is exempted by fiat, with no reason given
That 'needs a cause' and 'is uncaused' are labels handed out at will
ch1.breaks: The premise was never 'everything has a cause'. It is the narrower claim that whatever goes from potential to actual must be actualized by something already actual. Something with no potentiality is not an exception to that rule; it simply is not the kind of thing the rule is about.
ch1.reply: I never said everything has a cause. I said whatever goes from potential to actual needs something already actual to do it. God has no potentials, so there is nothing in him that could need actualizing — no cause needed, and none possible. Treating those two claims as the same is like saying that if all triangles have three sides, all shapes must.

ch1.title: Objection anatomy: Hume's uncaused coffee cup
ch1.caption: Hume says he can conceive of a thing popping into being uncaused. Two separate things go wrong — one about conceiving, one about what the scene even is.
ch1.where: Hume: we can conceive of something popping into existence uncaused
ch1.says: I can picture an empty room, then a coffee cup in it, with no cause anywhere in the picture. Whatever is conceivable is possible. So things can come to be uncaused, and your causal principle fails.
assumes: That picturing A without picturing B is conceiving A existing without B
That the scene can be described as a coming-to-be without using causal notions
That what the imagination can stage is a reliable map of what is possible
ch1.breaks: Leaving the cause out of your mental picture is not the same as putting 'no cause' into it. And, as Elizabeth Anscombe pressed, nothing in the bare picture makes it a case of coming into existence rather than being moved there from elsewhere — and the only thing that distinguishes those two is their causes.
ch1.reply: You can picture a man without picturing how tall he is, yet no man exists without some height. Your picture leaves the cause out; it doesn't show there is none. And tell me what makes your scene a cup coming into being rather than a cup teleported in from the kitchen — you'll find the only answer names a cause, which is exactly what you were trying to do without.

ch1.title: Objection anatomy: Kant on the limits of causality
ch1.caption: Grant that we learn causality from experience. The question is whether that limits where it applies. Compare how we learn geometry.
ch1.where: Kant: causality applies only within experience
ch1.says: We learn that things have causes by observing the world. Causality is a condition of our experience, so we have no right to stretch it beyond experience to an immaterial, timeless thing nobody could ever observe.
assumes: That a principle applies only where we first learned it
That we accept causality because we keep observing causes
That what cannot be observed is out of reason's reach
ch1.breaks: It confuses how we come to learn a principle with the range of things the principle is about. The reason things around us need actualizers is not that we observe them — it is that they are merely potential until made actual, and that reason is completely general.
ch1.reply: We learn geometry from ink drawings, but what we learn holds for figures of any colour, and of no colour at all. To say causality applies only to observable things is like saying Euclid applies only to figures you can see. What forces the conclusion here is that a potential cannot actualize itself — and that has nothing to do with whether anyone can look at it.

ch1.title: Objection anatomy: Newton's law of inertia
ch1.caption: The favourite scientific rebuttal: things keep moving with no cause. Three separate confusions are packed into it.
ch1.where: Newton’s law of inertia: motion continues without a cause
ch1.says: Newton showed that a body in motion stays in motion unless a force acts on it. So motion continues with no cause at all, and 'whatever is moved is moved by another' is dead physics.
assumes: That the proof is about what keeps bodies moving through time
That a law of nature is a thing that governs bodies, over and above them
That physics gives a complete inventory of what is in nature
ch1.breaks: The proof's real question is not what keeps a molecule moving but what makes these parts constitute a water molecule at this instant rather than loose atoms. Inertia presupposes that bodies with natures already exist; it cannot explain their existing.
ch1.reply: Inertia is shorthand for how a thing of a certain nature tends to behave. Fine — but why is there anything with that nature here and now? Newton's law assumes bodies; it does not supply them. And physics deliberately abstracts away causes to get equations it can solve, so its silence about them is a fact about the method, not a discovery about the world.

ch1.title: Objection anatomy: quantum events without causes
ch1.caption: Covers all three versions Feser answers — indeterminism, the Bell correlations, and particles in the vacuum. One slide does the damage in each.
ch1.where: Quantum indeterminism means some events have no cause
ch1.says: Quantum mechanics says an atom's decay, or the outcome of a measurement, has no determining prior cause. Some events just happen. So your principle of causality is refuted by physics itself.
assumes: That to cause something is to determine it
That if a theory doesn't mention a cause, there isn't one
That physics describes everything there is in what it describes
ch1.breaks: It slides from 'not deterministic' to 'not caused'. A cause need only make its effect intelligible, not inevitable. And a mathematical representation that was built by abstracting from causes will of course contain none — which tells us about the representation, not the world.
ch1.reply: Non-deterministic is not uncaused. A lead atom has a certain probability of decaying because of what it is — its nature is doing the work — and something still has to keep that atom in existence, with that nature, right now. Physics leaves causes out the way a black-and-white drawing leaves colour out: absence from the picture is not absence from the scene.

ch1.title: Objection anatomy: 'Aristotle was refuted centuries ago'
ch1.caption: The objection bundles Aristotle's physics and his metaphysics into one package. Separating them is the whole reply.
ch1.where: Aristotelianism was refuted by modern science
ch1.says: Aristotle thought the earth sat at the centre, that everything was made of four elements, that heavy things seek their natural place. Science buried all of it. An argument built on Aristotle is a museum piece.
assumes: That 'Aristotelianism' is one package that stands or falls together
That 'change is a potential made actual' is a scientific hypothesis
That an empirical result could in principle overturn it
ch1.breaks: It lumps Aristotle's dated astronomy and physics together with his metaphysics. Geocentrism was an empirical claim, and it lost. That change is the actualization of a potential is not an empirical claim at all — and every experiment already presupposes it.
ch1.reply: Yes, Aristotle's astronomy is dead, and good riddance. But 'change is a potential being made actual' isn't competing with any experiment; it is what doing an experiment already assumes, since setting one up and then reading the result means going from not knowing to knowing. You can't refute it with science, because doing science is an instance of it.

ch6a.title: Three ways a cause can have what it gives
ch6a.caption: A cause cannot give what it hasn't got — but 'having' comes in three grades. Feser's $20 example, laid out.
ch6a.where: The principle of proportionate causality: formally, virtually, eminently

columns.label: Formally
items: A $20 bill is in my wallet and I hand it to you
I am myself an instance of what you end up with
Fire is hot, and that is how it makes the pan hot

columns.label: Virtually
columns.sub: has the power to lay hands on it
items: No cash on me, but $20 sits in my bank account
I hold no bill; I hold the ability to get one
A boy need not have a black eye to give one

columns.label: Eminently
columns.sub: has something higher — can make it exist
items: I can have a genuine $20 bill printed on demand
Not getting hold of one — bringing one into being
A greater way of having it, not a lesser one

ch6a.note: Whatever is in an effect must be in its total cause in one of these three ways. Cottingham's counterexamples (helium from hydrogen, sponginess from eggs and flour) only ever look at the materials, and the principle was never about materials alone.

ch6a.title: Action follows being
ch6a.caption: The companion principle to proportionate causality: what a thing does can never outrun what it is. It is what closes the door on 'potential in God's activity'.
ch6a.where: Agere sequitur esse: action follows being

nodes.text: A thing's nature is what makes it the kind of thing it is
What a thing does flows from what it is
nodes.note: Eyes and ears work differently because they are built differently. Plants feed, grow and reproduce; stones do not, because stones are not alive.

nodes.text: So its activities cannot go beyond its nature
nodes.note: A stone cannot take in nutrients under its own power. Anything that could would not be a stone in the first place.

nodes.text: Otherwise the surplus activity would have no explanation
nodes.note: The same shape of reasoning as proportionate causality, shifted from efficient causes to natures.

nodes.text: Now: God's very existence is purely actual
So his acting cannot involve potentiality either
nodes.note: Existence is what is most basic about a thing; everything else follows from it. There is nowhere for potentials-for-activity to come from.

ch6a.title: Three ways to use a word
ch6a.caption: The distinction that lets us say something true about God without turning him into a large man or into a blank. Analogy is literal, not metaphor.
ch6a.where: The analogy of being: univocal, equivocal, analogical

columns.label: Univocal
columns.sub: exactly the same sense both times
items: 'Fido is a dog' and 'Rover is a dog'
One concept, applied in the very same way
Said of God: he becomes a bigger version of us

columns.label: Equivocal
items: 'A bat flew past' and 'I swung the bat'
Two unconnected concepts wearing one word
Said of God: the words carry no content at all

columns.label: Analogical
items: 'This wine is good' and 'George is a good man'
'I see the tree' and 'I see that the proof works'
Said of God: literal, positive, and not univocal

ch6a.note: Analogy was not invented to rescue theology. We already use it for goodness, life and seeing. Physics uses it too — calling one thing both wave and particle, or calling space itself curved.

ch6a.title: The argument that 'being' is analogical
ch6a.caption: Feser grounds analogy in the act/potency distinction from chapter 1 — so it stands independently of any argument for God.
ch6a.where: The argument that being is analogical

nodes.text: Actuality is real — it has being
nodes.note: Deny this and you are Heraclitus: nothing stable at all, not even the self who follows your argument to its conclusion.

nodes.text: Potentiality is real too — it has being
nodes.note: Deny this and you are Parmenides: change would be something out of nothing, and change cannot coherently be denied.

nodes.text: Potentiality is really distinct from actuality
If both had being in one sense, they would not be distinct
nodes.note: Then potentiality would just be a kind of actuality, or the other way round.

nodes.text: If potentiality's sense were unrelated, it would be unreal
Univocal, equivocal, analogical exhaust the options
So 'being' is said of things analogically
nodes.note: Which is why we can say something literal and positive about a God who shares no genus with anything we have met.

ch6a.title: Five proofs, one God
ch6a.caption: Each of these descriptions holds if and only if the others do. So the five arguments do not stack up five deities — they circle one, seen from five angles.

root.note: The terminus of the Aristotelian proof of chapter 1. Every branch below is equivalent to it, and each is where a different proof ended up.

branches.text: Absolutely simple — the One of chapter 2
branches.why: Anything with parts is only potentially a whole until combined, so what is purely actual has no parts. And whatever is simple can have no merely potential part. Each entails the other.
Where essence and existence differ they stand as potential to actual. Pure actuality rules that out, so here essence just is existence. And what just is existence cannot depend on anything.
Contingency would mean a potential for existence waiting to be actualized, or parts waiting to be combined. Neither is on offer. And a necessary being can have neither.
The Augustinian proof needs universals, numbers and propositions to reside in a necessarily existing mind — and there is only one necessary being to be that mind.

branches.text: Unique — there cannot be a second
branches.why: Two of a kind need genus plus difference, or matter plus essence, and that means parts and so potentiality. With no parts, there is nothing left to tell a second one apart.

ch6a.title: What follows from pure actuality and simplicity
ch6a.caption: Every attribute in this chapter is read off one root. Simplicity is not a curiosity bolted on at the end — it is what makes God God rather than the greatest creature.
ch6a.where: Simplicity: the heart of classical theism

root.text: Purely actual, and so absolutely simple
root.note: Two ways of saying one thing: whatever has parts is potential until combined, and whatever has no potentiality can have no parts.

branches.why: A second would need some feature marking it off, and any such feature means genus and difference, or matter and essence — parts, and so potentiality.

branches.text: Simple — no parts, not even essence and existence
branches.why: Parts are merely potentially combined until something combines them, and that something would be a cause of God. A first cause can have no cause.
Real change needs both potentiality (something to be actualized) and parts (something that stays while something else goes). God has neither.
Matter just is the potentiality to take on form, and every material thing has parts that could be rearranged. Even fundamental particles come to be and pass away.

branches.text: Eternal — outside time, not merely everlasting
branches.why: In time he would add new moments to his life, act one way then another, and have distinct stages as parts. All of that is change and composition.
To be contingent is to have a potential for existence needing actualization, or parts needing combination. Neither applies to what is purely actual.

branches.text: Alive, in the fullest possible way
branches.why: To be alive is to act from an inner principle rather than being pushed about from outside. Animals must still eat and breathe; nothing whatever acts on God.

ch6a.title: Drill: classical theism or superhero god?
ch6a.caption: Theistic personalism keeps the word 'God' but makes him a member of a kind — a person like us with the limits removed. Twelve statements: which picture is each one describing?
ch6a.prompt: Does this describe the God of classical theism, or a superhero god?

items.text: A person like us, but without our limits on power and knowledge
items.why: This makes God one species under the genus person — a member of a kind, and so composite.

items.text: Not one being among beings, but subsistent existence itself
items.why: He is not an item on the list of things that exist; he is why there is a list.

items.text: His power and his knowledge are two really distinct things in him
items.why: Two real constituents are parts, and parts need something to combine them — which would be a cause of God.

items.text: Whatever we truly say of him we say analogically, not univocally
items.why: 'Wise' said of Socrates and of God are related but not identical. Plantinga's critique assumes otherwise.

items.text: He changes his mind when circumstances change
items.why: Change is a potential actualized. Process theologians accept this openly; a purely actual God cannot.

items.text: There could not even in principle be a second one of him
items.why: Not a lucky fact about how many gods there happen to be. With no parts, nothing could differentiate a rival.

items.text: He is extremely powerful — the most powerful being there happens to be
items.why: 'Happens to be' makes his supremacy a contingent fact rather than what he is.

items.text: He is the reason anything at all exists at this very instant
items.why: Ultimacy, not merely superiority. This is the God the five proofs actually reach.

items.text: Immaterial, so a kind of very great spirit or superangel
items.why: Immaterial but still composite is a grander creature, not God. Feser says worshipping it would be idolatry.

items.text: His essence and his existence are not two things in him
items.why: He does not have existence; he is existence. Anything else would need a cause for the joining.

items.text: He has a nature, which he possesses the way we possess ours
items.why: Having a nature, rather than being it, means essence and existence come apart — and something must join them.

items.text: Immutable — and creating the world worked no change in him
items.why: The change is in the world, which now exists. Becoming Creator is a Cambridge change, not a real one.

ch6a.title: Eternal, not merely everlasting
ch6a.caption: Most people imagine God's eternity as unlimited longevity. Feser means something stronger and stranger: no location in time at all.
ch6a.where: Eternity: no beginning, no end — and no time

columns.label: Everlasting
columns.sub: inside time, but for all of it
items: Existed at every past moment, will exist at every future one
Keeps adding new seconds, days and years to his life
Learns it is now Tuesday, then learns it is now Wednesday
Has earlier and later stages — and stages are parts

columns.label: Eternal
items: At no moment at all, so before and after do not apply
Nothing is ever added; there are no stages to add to
One single act, not one act now and another later
Causing a world with a history is not having a history

ch6a.note: Feser's image: an author who conceives a whole novel in a single flash of insight. Inside the story the middle follows the beginning, but he did not think of the beginning first. God causes what exists at every time, in one act, without acting first at one time and then at another.

ch6a.title: Objection anatomy: anthropomorphic or empty?
ch6a.caption: A clean-looking dilemma with a hidden third option. Spotting it is the whole point of the analogy of being.
ch6a.where: God-talk is either anthropomorphic or empty
ch6a.says: Either your words about God mean what they normally mean, in which case your God is a very large man in the sky, or they don't, in which case you are making noises with no content. Take your pick.
assumes: That a word is used either in exactly the same sense or in totally unrelated ones
That any non-univocal use is metaphor, and so not literal
That analogy is a device invented to get theologians off this hook
ch6a.breaks: It offers two roads where there are three. Between univocal and equivocal usage lies analogy — and analogy of attribution and of proper proportionality are literal uses, not figures of speech. We rely on them already, outside theology, for goodness, life, seeing, and for being itself.
ch6a.reply: There's a third option you left out. When I call wine good and a man good, I'm not saying one thing twice, and I'm not equivocating the way 'bat' does in baseball and in a cave. I'm speaking analogically — literally, by a real proportion: the wine stands to what wine is for as the man stands to what a man is for. Divine power is like that. Not Zeus's biceps, and not a blank.

ch6a.title: Objection anatomy: Plantinga on simplicity
ch6a.caption: The most cited philosophical objection to divine simplicity. Feser's answer is that it imports three assumptions no classical theist holds.
ch6a.where: Plantinga: simplicity makes God a single property — an abstract object
ch6a.says: If God is identical with each of his properties, then all his properties are identical with one another, so he has exactly one. But plainly he has several — power and mercy aren't the same thing. And if God is a property, God is an abstract object, and abstract objects don't create worlds.
assumes: That 'property' covers everything we can predicate — essence, properties, contingent accidents, bare relations
That properties are Platonic abstract objects that a thing participates in
That 'God is wise' and 'Socrates is wise' use 'wise' in the same sense
ch6a.breaks: Classical theists reject all three. They distinguish a thing's essence from its properties, its properties from its contingent accidents, and its intrinsic accidents from mere relations. They hold these are concrete constituents of the thing, not items in a third realm. And they say power and knowledge are said of God analogically. Take those three away and the objection has nothing to stand on.
ch6a.reply: Nobody in this tradition says God is a property. That word is carrying far too much in your objection — you've swept essence, properties, accidents and relations into one bin and then put the bin in Plato's heaven. Aquinas does neither. And since 'knowledge' and 'power' are said of God analogically, the fact that they're two different things in us is no reason to think they're two different things in him.

ch6a.title: Objection anatomy: a personal God needn't be simple
ch6a.caption: Theistic personalism's core move, and why Feser thinks it costs far more than its defenders notice.
ch6a.where: Theistic personalism: a personal God need not be simple
ch6a.says: God is a person. Persons have natures, have distinct attributes, make free choices, respond to what we do. A partless God with no real properties isn't a person at all — he's an inert abstraction. Keep the personal God and drop the medieval simplicity talk.
assumes: That being personal requires being a member of the kind 'person'
That simplicity can be dropped with nothing else going with it
That classical theists deny God is personal
ch6a.breaks: The dispute was never personal versus impersonal — classical theists attribute intellect and will to God too. It is whether God falls under a genus. And simplicity is not detachable: whatever has parts needs something to combine them, so a composite God would require a cause, could not be the first cause, and could in principle have a twin.
ch6a.reply: I agree God has intellect and will. What I deny is that he is one species of a kind called 'person', standing alongside you, me and the angels. Make him that and he is composite — which means something had to put him together, and there could have been two of him. What you'd be holding is a superangel, and none of the five proofs ever delivered one of those.

ch6a.title: Objection anatomy: necessary and contingent in God
ch6a.caption: Morris's objection, and the distinction between a real change and a merely Cambridge change that answers it.
ch6a.where: Necessary and contingent properties can’t be identical
ch6a.says: God is necessarily omnipotent but only contingently the creator — he could have refrained from making anything. So he has both necessary and contingent properties. A necessary property can't be identical with a contingent one, so not all God's properties are identical. Simplicity fails.
assumes: That being the creator is a real feature of God, on a par with omnipotence
That every true description of a thing marks some real feature in it
ch6a.breaks: It runs together real properties and what Geach called Cambridge properties. When Plato grows taller it becomes true that Socrates is shorter than Plato — but nothing at all changed in Socrates. Simplicity says God has no contingent real properties. It never said he has no contingent Cambridge properties.
ch6a.reply: Being creator is a Cambridge property, like Socrates becoming the shorter of the two. What actually changed is the world, which now exists — not God. Simplicity claims that God's real features are all one; 'having created' was never one of them, so your two descriptions were never rival candidates for being identical.

ch6a.title: Objection anatomy: 'to act is to change'
ch6a.caption: The standard objection to immutability. It commits a fallacy logicians have had a name for since antiquity.
ch6a.says: When I type, my fingers move, my neurons fire, my thoughts shift. Acting always changes the one acting, not just the thing acted on. So if God creates, God changes — and your immutable God is a contradiction.
assumes: That because every agent we have met changes while acting, every possible agent must
That what is essential to acting is the agent's own alteration
ch6a.breaks: A fallacy of accident: turning a feature that happens to accompany the cases we know into a feature of the thing as such. Every college professor who ever lived was under nine feet tall; that sets no limit on possible professors. What is essential to acting is producing an effect in another thing, not being altered oneself.
ch6a.reply: We change when we act because we are limited — I have to move my fingers to get words onto the screen. That's a fact about me, not about acting. What acting is, is bringing about an effect in something else. Teaching is making someone learn; whether by lecturing or by writing is incidental. God's creating is simply his causing the world to be.

ch6a.title: Objection anatomy: acting at t1 and at t2
ch6a.caption: A sharp objection to divine timelessness, defused by noticing where the date in the sentence really belongs.
ch6a.where: Causing at t1 and at t2 means acting in time
ch6a.says: You say God holds everything in being at every moment. Then he acts in 469 BC and he acts again in 1961. Anything that acts at one time and then at another is in time. So a timeless God cannot be sustaining a temporal world.
assumes: That 'God causes X to exist at t' means the same as 'at t, God causes X to exist'
That one cause with effects at many times must itself be spread across those times
ch6a.breaks: It slides the time index off the effect and onto the cause. Those two sentences are not equivalent. God's single timeless act causes a world that has a history; it is not a series of acts strung out along that history, one per moment.
ch6a.reply: Watch where the date sits. Saying God causes something to exist in 1961 is not saying that in 1961 God did something. Picture an author who sees a whole novel in one flash: inside the book chapter two follows chapter one, but he did not think chapter one first and chapter two later. In one act, God causes a world in which things happen at different times.
